programs.author: Digital Larry
programs.description: Delay program for the FV-1. Explore the documented controls below; the source header contains implementation notes.

license.label: Public source; no explicit licence identified

comments.text:
Here's the idea of an oil-can delay. It uses a drum which is insulating but has a conductive outer surface. It runs through a reservoir of oil and a brush contact connected to a voltage amplifier from the input writes electrons onto the surface which are picked up by another brush on the other side of the drum. So the delay time is related to the angular displacement of the brushes and the RPM. For example if the brushes are 180 degrees apart, and it's going 60 RPM (1 rev/second) then that is a 500 msec delay. t (seconds) = (angle/360) * 60/RPM = angle / (6 * RPM). Faster the RPM, the shorter the delay.

Next there is a wobble (LFO chorus) due to the drum being off center. The rate of this corresponds to the RPM or revs per second. Faster the RPM, the faster the chorus LFO.

So we need an inverse relationship between chorus rate and delay time from one pot which controls the delay time setting. This you can see from the inverted scale going to the chorus block lfo rate input from pot1 which also goes through a smoother. The net effect of changing the scale/offset blocks (or the delay max time, or the chorus LFO max rate) is to change the angular displacement of the read and write brushes. If the specifics are important, figure it out but you can get different sounds by changing these ratios. Interestingly, the "size" of the drum makes no difference.

I used the multi-tap delay block because supposedly some oil can delays had two heads, but I'm not sure.

Pot0 = delay time/lfo rate (limited range setting, try making it longer if you like)
Pot1 = chorus width
Pot2 = feedback
This sounds really nice, and takes on a very 'rubbery' sound to it when you crank up the chorus width

upstream_metadata.name: Improved Octave Up
upstream_metadata.author: Don Stavely
upstream_metadata.description: This solves for the 'crossfade cancellation' issue...

comments.text:
;Folks who have played with the pitch-shift routine for octave-up and octave-down know about the "crossfade phase cancellation" issue.
;For octave-down, you get a tremolo effect due to the slower ramp speed (-8192). But for octave-up, the fast ramp (16384) results in an unpleasant warble.
;We can't use a longer delay than 4096, so we are stuck with it, right?

;Here is a trick I just came up with: Do two pitch shifts in a row, each shifting up by the square root of two.
;The magic ramp speed is 6783. Voila, an octave up with a pleasing tremolo instead of the warble.
;It requires another 4096 memory and 8 instructions, but still only 1 ramp (so you can still use the other for octave down, etc).

;Yes, the tradeoff is latency. In the application I am working on I am going for more of a chorus effect - i.e. multiple instruments rather than a single instrument like a 12-string.

;Notice that I write 512 words into the 4096-word delay. This reduces the latency by that amount.
;The reason you can do this is that the crossfade waveform is zero for the first 1/8th of the delay. If you try a 2048 word delay you will have to change the "wra delay1+512,0" to "wra delay1+256, 0" in both places. This is probably why it sounded worse than the standard single-step 4096 algorithm.

;Frank commented in an older thread that this trick of writing 1/8th of the way into the buffer shouldn't work.
;I assure you (and Frank) that does. It is totally glitchless, and reduces the average latency by 1/4 for free. I don't think Frank considered it carefully.

comments.text:
The Choirsaw (mono edition) is a bit on the bizarre side. It's a delay at its core but combines pitch shifting and tremolo. The result is something pretty unique and also musically interesting.

P0 sets the delay time from long to short (about 800ms to a few ms). It also cross-fades into the
pitch-shift as it is turned up. So, when the delay gets shorter more pitch shift is available in the
feedback path.

octaves increase.

P2 sets the sinewave tremolo speed from 0 - slow - fast. This gets really interesting when you set the delay to slow, feedback high and trem fast. Try it!

comments.text:
This routine is based on Mick Taylor's (Ice-9s) reverb loop
and shimmer code with some changes such as:

1) Prime numbers for delay line lengths.
2) More linear mapping of pot sweep to reverb time.
3) Anti-aliasing filter before the pitch-shifter.
4) Shimmer level is controlled by feeding both the input signal
   and the reverb output into the pitch-shifter in varying amounts.
5) Pitch-shifted signal is fed into a delay line to give a couple of short delays.
   This lets the shimmer effect build up slowly in time.
6) Output is 100% wet.  Uncomment line at bottom to add dry signal.

;POT0 = Reverb time (0 to 10 seconds).
;POT1 = Amount of treble in reverb loop.

programs.name: Wavetable Thief
programs.author: Andreas Jansson
programs.description: Every note gets robbed. Moments after the attack the thief listens for the newest note's period; once it hears the same equal-tempered semitone three times running, it steals exactly four periods of the note (two below C3, one below C2) into a loop that plays on as a static digital oscillator: the note's own waveform, frozen, in tune, with no flutter. If it can't hear a clean period (a chord, a smear) it steals a whole moment instead, a short loop of the sound that stutters on like a frozen tape. The loot plays on one side and its shadow on the other: the same loop at half speed, an octave down and darker. Every theft makes the two trade places in a quick glide across the field, so the bright loot and the dark shadow ping-pong from note to note and over a phrase both sides get both. The next note robs again, and a held note gets robbed again every second, each time a later, darker cycle. Left alone, a stolen tone slowly darkens from its bright attack to the body of the note. Your playing feeds the thief's greed: sparse playing lets the loot fade like a plucked note, steady playing holds it, and a busy patch makes it greedy, the held loops swelling until they clip into hard, buzzing squares; over 20 to 30 s of playing the sound rots from clean stolen tones to fuzz. Stop, and the last theft rings on for a moment and dies away within a second or two.

programs.name: Pitch-Locked Decimator
programs.author: Andreas Jansson
programs.description: A pitch tracker finds the note under your playing, and a sample-and-hold chops the sound a whole number of times per period of that note, so all the crunch lands on its harmonics: a lo-fi chip voice that stays in tune. Every phrase starts clean and travels down a staircase: the clean sound crossfades into the chip at 16 samples per period, then 8, then it is crushed through and through at 4 and 2 samples per period, a raw square-wave buzz, and then it climbs back up the same way to clean and starts again, so even a stream of notes with no gaps keeps cycling. Fall sets how long it slides. Past a quarter turn the rumble keeps going, and every half second the snow loses one more bit, grinding from powder to grit; at full Fall, about seven seconds in, the last of it is pure 1-bit. Over the last stages a reverb opens around the slide: a small room at first, it grows with every stage into a huge, smooth hall, and the slide sinks under it until the hall is the whole sound. The hall stays while the slope is wiped and through the quiet after it, and the next note you play cuts it off dead. Snow sets how much the pack holds: turn it up and it takes longer to tip. Stop playing and the pack hangs for a few seconds, then slides by itself.

programs.author: Andreas Jansson
programs.description: A drum machine for effects, running at the tempo you set with Time. Each step of the 11-step pattern holds one of four moves on the last quarter step: a deep drawl two octaves down, a double repeat an octave down, a four-fold stutter at pitch or an eight-fold roll an octave up, forward on the left and backwards on the right. programs.name: Mitosis
programs.author: Andreas Jansson
programs.description: The first note you play into an empty dish founds a culture: its first quarter second is frozen as a cell, and you hear the founder at once. After one cycle the cell divides: a daughter an octave up on the left and her mirror twin an octave down on the right. Every cycle the culture divides again: the clones double in number and come twice as fast, up to thirty-two in a cycle, and their octaves spread up to three either way, always mirrored: when the left clone climbs, the right one sinks. Your playing is the food. Every attack feeds the culture, and each division costs more than the last. When food runs short, or the culture reaches its peak, it dies back a generation per cycle, the clones thinning out. Meanwhile the dish keeps the newest note you played, and the moment the last cell dies that note takes over as the founder of the next culture, so the waves run back to back with no gap: one note, a swarm of its clones, the next note. Stop playing and the culture fades away with your sound; it races through the rest of its life unheard, and the dish waits for your next note.

programs.name: Tesseract
programs.author: Andreas Jansson
programs.description: The sixteen corners of a tesseract are sixteen ways to replay a slice of what you just played: left or right, forwards or backwards, at pitch or an octave down, from two or four slices back. On every step the cube turns to a new corner, and you hear that corner on the left and the corner opposite it on the right, which is different in every way: a slice played forwards at pitch from close by on one side is answered by a slice reversed an octave down from further back on the other. As the cube turns, the pair walks a tour of all the corners, and the tour is a pattern that repeats: sixteen steps when it turns by one corner, eight, four, and at eight corners a step it flips straight to the opposite corner. Your notes spin it: each note speeds the turning up, so the tour gets shorter and wilder while you play, and when it passes half a turn a step it snaps still and starts spinning up again; rests let it slow down. No clock needed: Time is the time between steps, like the clock pulse of the _clk version, from 0.05 s to 2 s. Slices are as long as a step up to a quarter second; on slower steps each slice stays a quarter second long and the rest of the step is a rest. Turn sets how it turns on its own (0: it rests between notes), Spin how hard each note pushes it.

programs.name: Zeno's Arrow
programs.author: Andreas Jansson
programs.description: Zeno's paradox on a beat you set. An arrow catches what you play the moment it is fired and plays it back an octave down and slowed to half speed, then again at pitch in half the time, then an octave up in a quarter of the time, two octaves up in an eighth, each repeat thrown to the other side: a ping-pong that accelerates and climbs and lands exactly on the step it was aimed at. The arrows themselves follow Zeno too: the phrase is 16 steps, and each arrow flies half of what is left, 8 steps, then 4, 2, 1 and a last quick one, so a slow, deep flight is followed by shorter and shorter ones until the phrase lands in a flurry, and the next long flight starts. There is no clock to patch: the Time knob is the step, one every 0.05 s to 2 s (300 bpm sixteenths to 30 bpm quarters), and the steps run on steadily by themselves, just as a clock patched into the clocked twin would. Your notes are the payload and choose the height: a loud note keeps halving up to the 30 ms limit, a soft one climbs a step or two, and a rest stays low and slow.
